fixes.explanation: Yes, friend, count it up. For the older men, Paul lists a whole run of things: temperate, dignified, self-controlled, and sound in faith, love, and perseverance. For the younger men, it's one line: "…urge the younger men to be self-controlled." Short and to the point.

That's what Paul says, friend. He wants Titus's teaching above reproach "…so that anyone who opposes us will be ashamed, having nothing bad to say about us." If the critic looks for something to pounce on and comes up empty, that's a quiet kind of win.

Yes, friend. Paul says "…in every respect they will adorn the teaching about God our Savior." Adorn is a decorating word, so their good faith is like decoration on the teaching. And he says in EVERY respect, so none of it is left plain.

Elijah the prophet (1 Kings 18:36) is a great name, friend, but he's not the one Paul has in mind. The verse says we await "…glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ." Paul names Jesus Christ, plain as day.

Moses, Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10), is a giant of the faith, friend, but he's not who Paul points to here. Paul says we await "…glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ." The hope is Jesus, and Paul says so outright.
That's the word, friend. Paul says, "Let no one despise you." Titus is to speak with all authority, and Paul doesn't want anyone looking down on him. Strong last word to Titus in this chapter.
Flattery sounds pleasant, friend, so I see the pull. But Paul says, "Let no one despise you." He's talking about being looked down on, not about being praised. That's the line he leaves Titus with.
